svg.title: Special use airspace: what a VFR pilot does
svg.desc: Table of prohibited, restricted, warning, military operations and alert areas with how each is charted and what a VFR pilot does. Prohibited and restricted areas need permission of the using or controlling agency when active, under 14 CFR 91.133. A military operations area needs no permission but extreme caution when active. Warning areas lie over international waters starting 3 nautical miles from the coast. Alert areas have high volumes of pilot training or unusual aerial activity. Details are in the chart margin and NOTAMs.
svg.text: Special use airspace: what a VFR pilot does
Charted blue: prohibited, restricted, warning. Magenta: alert and MOA. Details are in the chart margin.
Prohibited
P- (for example P-56)
Flight is not allowed without the permission
of the using agency (14 CFR 91.133).
Restricted
R- (for example R-2301)
Hazards such as artillery or missiles. Permission of the using
or controlling agency is needed when active (91.133).
When it is not active you may transit.
Warning
W- (for example W-291)
Starts 3 NM from the U.S. coast. Hazards to
nonparticipating aircraft, like a restricted area.
MOA
charted by name
Military training. No permission needed, but use
extreme caution when active; ask ATC or FSS.
Alert
A- (for example A-211)
High volume of pilot training or unusual aerial
activity. All pilots share the responsibility.
Controlled firing areas are not charted: activity stops if a spotter sees an aircraft. Check NOTAMs too.
Source: 14 CFR 91.133; AIM 3-4; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide.
